name: auger-flighting-spoil
title: Auger Flighting Spoil
description: A continuous-work loader: a helical auger scrolls its flighting texture while material discharges at the top and free-falls into a growing spoil pile whose silhouette is governed by a real 37deg angle-of-repose check — the accumulating byproduct, not the spinning tube, is the primary read.
useWhen: a continuous-work indicator whose loop needs a legible accumulating BYPRODUCT to prove ongoing work, not just a spinning glyph — pick loader-thread-spool instead when the indicator must also carry a real determinate/indeterminate progress contract (bytes loaded of a known total) with ARIA progressbar semantics, since auger-flighting-spoil has no notion of a total or completion, only an unbounded steady-state loop; pick loader-spirograph-trace instead when a determinate percentage on a fixed decorative route matters more than an accumulating material byproduct.
instruction: A 2D canvas loader rendering a continuous-flight auger feeding a growing spoil pile. Every extent (tube position, tube width, drop point, spoil-zone span, particle radius, gravity scale) is a fraction of S = min(container width, container height) and centred on the container's centre point, so the whole scene scales as one unit and a tall-narrow card never distorts the pile's available spread relative to its height. The auger tube is a vertical rect (width 0.13S) whose top sits at cy-0.34S and bottom at cy+0.1S, clipped and filled with a repeating diagonal two-tone band texture: each pitch (0.45 x tube-width, giving ~7-8 visible turns over the tube's height) is split into two half-pitch bands, BOTH drawn with the SAME --foreground token at two widely separated alphas (0.18 and 0.55) rather than crossing two different tokens — a single token composites monotonically against --background in either theme, so the step between bands is guaranteed to survive a theme flip instead of two different tokens happening to composite to the same value in one theme. The scroll offset advances every frame by pitch-length x 0.833 rev/s x dt (50 RPM) — a continuous sub-pixel-per-frame texture scroll, never a discrete per-flight-turn geometry step, which is what keeps a real 50 RPM rotation from aliasing against a ~60Hz paint into a strobe; the real RPM sets scroll SPEED only. The initial offset is seeded to an arbitrary fractional phase (never zero), so the texture is never caught aligned to its own start. A short static chute line runs from the tube's top to a fixed drop point 1.6 tube-widths to the right, from which one particle is spawned every 420ms (slow enough to watch each one fall and land individually) at a slightly jittered x and free-falls straight down under a gravity constant of 800px/s^2 scaled by S/400 (so fall duration reads consistently regardless of card size or aspect ratio). Landing is resolved against a 26-column heightmap spanning a spoil zone 0.9S wide, centred on the drop point (not the container) with real slack on both flanks for a full 85%-cap cone at the 37deg repose angle; a falling particle's column is derived from its jittered x, and it settles the instant it reaches that column's current surface height, keeping its render x rather than snapping to the column centre so the pile texture stays granular. Each landing adds a fixed contribution (capHeight x 0.045) to its column, then a relax pass enforces the 37deg angle-of-repose limit by transferring height between any adjacent columns whose difference exceeds columnWidth x tan(37deg) — repeated until stable — which is what turns a straight-down discharge into a symmetric cone (apex under the drop point) instead of a spike. The pile's outline is redrawn every frame as a filled path connecting each column's current surface point, plus individual particle dots (falling, settled, and fading) layered on top for texture. Once the tallest column reaches 85% of the available spoil-zone height, every subsequent landing also retires the single oldest still-settled dot: it fades over 600ms and, on completing, its contribution is subtracted from its column's height and a relax pass re-smooths the resulting dip, holding the pile in steady-state turnover (new landings balanced by old retirements) rather than ever overflowing past the cap, collapsing into a crater at the apex, or shrinking back to nothing. At mount the pile is pre-seeded to 40% of cap height (a symmetric cone computed in closed form, apex under the drop column) with a few particles already mid-fall, so t0 never reads as an empty start; by ~2.5s roughly six more particles have landed and the silhouette has visibly grown and reshaped; by ~5s the pile is at or near the 85% cap with the retire-fade cycle visibly running (one dot fading out as another lands), which is the visible difference between the build-up phase and the steady-state phase that makes the loop read as alive and unbounded rather than a process that finishes. Colours are read via getComputedStyle(document.documentElement) for --foreground/--ns-muted before the first paint (no colour-literal fallback — an empty read means "not ready," and the draw call itself re-attempts the read and bails without painting rather than falling back to a hardcoded value), cached, and refreshed by a MutationObserver on documentElement's class attribute; the tube outline and helix bands use --foreground value steps, the pile fill and settled/retiring dots use --ns-muted, falling dots use --foreground, and --ns-accent is never touched anywhere in the component. Canvas is sized via ResizeObserver reading the container's actual box (devicePixelRatio-scaled, CSS pixel style dimensions set explicitly) and every geometric constant is rederived from that measurement, so the pile always resolves at card scale regardless of aspect ratio. An IntersectionObserver pauses the rAF loop when the card scrolls offscreen and resumes it cleanly on return. `autoplay: none` because the loop runs on its own internal clock with no pointer/scroll/press input to drive. Under prefers-reduced-motion the component renders exactly one static frame, re-attempting the token read on every animation frame until colours are available: the pile pre-seeded directly to a full symmetric 85%-height cone with settled dots sprinkled across its surface (no build-up, matching the live pile's granular texture rather than a smooth triangle), the helix drawn at a fixed unmoving offset, and no particles in flight — the most structured, most legible single frame of the mechanic — and no rAF loop is ever started once painted. Cleanup on unmount cancels the pending rAF, disconnects the MutationObserver/ResizeObserver/IntersectionObserver, and clears all pending timers. Zero dependencies, canvas + CSS only, no WebGL context to drop. Differs from loader-thread-spool's spinner-with-trail mechanic: nothing here spins in place or converts into a gauge — the tube's rotation is a fixed, minor background cue, and the spoil pile's cumulative silhouette is the entire point.
